_comment: Structured per-state voter information. Status supports four values (placeholder, in_review, verified, needs_review) at both the state level and independently per section, so a future automated checker can flag a single section (or the whole state) as needs_review without touching 'content'/'source_url'/'last_verified' — those represent the last published, human-verified instruction and are never auto-cleared. A checker only ever writes status/flagged_reason/flagged_at. 'content' is null until real information is verified and added — the page renders its own 'not yet available' copy for null content rather than storing 51x15 copies of the same placeholder sentence here.

next_state_election.name: New Hampshire State Primary Election
next_state_election.source_name: NH Secretary of State — 2026-2027 Political Calendar

glance_notes.text: New Hampshire's General Election — including the Governor's race and the state Legislature — falls on the same day as the federal general election, November 3, 2026.
glance_notes.source_name: NH Secretary of State — 2026-2027 Political Calendar

register.label: Register to Vote
register.content: You can register to vote in New Hampshire if you're a U.S. citizen, at least 18 years old on Election Day, and a resident of the town or city ward where you want to register — there's no minimum length of time you need to have lived there first. You'll complete a Voter Registration Form with your local town/city clerk or supervisors of the checklist, and provide proof of your identity, age, U.S. citizenship, and domicile (primary residence). Acceptable proof includes a driver's license, government-issued photo ID, or passport for identity and age; a birth certificate, passport, or naturalization papers for citizenship; and a driver's license, vehicle registration, or a government-issued bill/check/tax document showing your address for domicile. Student ID cards cannot be used as proof for any of these registration requirements. If you don't have documents for one or more requirements, ask your local clerk or supervisors of the checklist — they can help, including checking existing state records with your permission. New Hampshire does not offer online voter registration; you register in person (before or on Election Day) or by absentee if you qualify.
register.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Register to Vote

check_registration.label: Check Voter Registration
check_registration.content: Use the Secretary of State's Voter Information Lookup to check whether you're registered, confirm your party affiliation, and — if you've requested one — track the status of an absentee ballot. You can also contact your local town/city clerk or supervisors of the checklist directly.

deadlines.label: Registration Deadlines
deadlines.content: In-person registration (at your clerk's office or a supervisors-of-the-checklist meeting) closes 6–13 days before an election — the exact day varies by town, so check with your local clerk or the Voter Information Lookup. If you miss that window, New Hampshire still lets you register at your polling place on Election Day itself, as long as you're in line by the time polls close. If you're registering by mailed absentee request, your request must reach your clerk by 12:00 p.m. the day before the election. If you want to change your party affiliation before a state primary, that must be done before the first Wednesday in June preceding the election (RSA 654:34, IV).
deadlines.glance_value: 6–13 days before Election Day, or same-day at the polls
deadlines.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Registration Deadlines

polling_place.label: Find a Polling Place
polling_place.content: Look up your polling place with the Secretary of State's Voter Information Lookup — the same tool also shows your sample ballot once it's available. Polling locations can occasionally change between elections, so it's worth checking shortly before each one even if you've voted at the same place before. If the tool doesn't show a location for your address, contact your town or city clerk directly.

election_day.label: Election Day Voting
election_day.content: At your polling place, announce your name and address to a ballot clerk. If you're already registered, you'll be asked to show a qualifying photo ID (see Voter ID Requirements below) before receiving your ballot; an election official who personally knows you may also verify your identity in place of an ID. If your name isn't on the checklist, you can register on the spot — see Registration Deadlines — as long as you're in line before the polls close.
election_day.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Election Day Voting

polling_hours.label: Polling Hours
polling_hours.content: State law (RSA 659:4) requires polls to open no later than 11:00 a.m. and close no earlier than 7:00 p.m. — those are legal limits, not a fixed daily schedule. The actual opening and closing times are set locally: cities decide their own polling hours (within those limits) at least 30 days before a state election, and towns can vote to adjust their hours the same way. Exact hours vary by municipality — always confirm your town or city's specific hours through the Voter Information Lookup or your local clerk rather than assuming a single statewide time.
polling_hours.source_name: RSA 659:4, Hours of Polling in Municipalities (official NH statute text)

early_voting.label: Early Voting
early_voting.content: To vote before Election Day in New Hampshire, the Secretary of State's guidance describes absentee voting as the option — either by mail, or in person at your town/city clerk's office. Either way requires a qualifying reason under one of the state's specific excuses (see Absentee & Mail Voting below); it is not open to any voter without one, unlike some states' no-excuse early voting.
early_voting.glance_value: Absentee only, with a qualifying reason
early_voting.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Absentee Ballots

absentee_mail.label: Absentee & Mail Voting
absentee_mail.content: You can vote absentee, by mail or in person at your town/city clerk's office, if you're unable to vote in person on Election Day because: you'll be out of town; you have a religious observance, physical disability, or illness that prevents voting in person; an employment obligation or caregiving duty keeps you away for the entire time polls are open; you're confined in a penal institution for a misdemeanor or awaiting trial; you're enrolled in the Attorney General's Address Confidentiality Program or protected by a domestic violence protective order; or the National Weather Service has issued a winter storm, blizzard, or ice storm warning for your town on Election Day. You can request an absentee ballot up to six months before the election (for the 2026 State Primary, starting March 8, 2026; for the 2026 General Election, starting May 3, 2026 — this six-month window doesn't apply to military/overseas voters, see below). The deadline to request a ballot is 12:00 p.m. the day before the election by mail, or 5:00 p.m. the day before in person. Since September 30, 2025, requesting an absentee ballot also requires proving your identity: either include a photocopy of your photo ID with a mailed request, show photo ID in person, or have your application notarized. Completed ballots must reach your clerk by 5:00 p.m. on Election Day, whether mailed or delivered in person — the U.S. Postal Service recommends mailing at least a week ahead, so request your ballot at least two weeks before Election Day if you're relying on the mail. Track your request and ballot status anytime with the Voter Information Lookup.
absentee_mail.glance_value: Must qualify; request by 12pm mail / 5pm in person, day before
absentee_mail.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Absentee Ballots

voter_id.label: Voter ID Requirements
voter_id.content: New Hampshire has two separate identification requirements — one to register, and a different one to vote once you're registered — and it's worth keeping them straight. Registering to vote: you must prove identity, age, U.S. citizenship, and domicile using the documents listed under Register to Vote above; student ID cards do not satisfy this requirement. Voting at the polls (RSA 659:13): once registered, you must show one of the following to receive a ballot: a driver's license from any state or the federal government; a non-driver ID card from NH DMV or another state's motor vehicle agency; a “voting identification only” photo ID card issued by NH DMV; a U.S. armed services ID card; a U.S. passport or passport card; or — if you're already registered and personally known to them — verification of your identity by a town/city/ward moderator, clerk, supervisor of the checklist, or selectman (this option is only available for already-registered voters checking in, never as proof when registering). An acceptable photo ID can be expired for up to 5 years and still count; voters 65 or older can use an otherwise-qualifying ID regardless of expiration. The name on the ID must substantially match the name on the checklist. Student ID cards are not accepted as voter ID: under a 2026 law change (Chapter 243, SB 223-FN, effective August 31, 2026 — covering the September 8, 2026 State Primary onward), student identification cards are no longer an acceptable form of voter ID at the polls, a change from the prior rule. If you don't have an approved ID, you will not be allowed to vote until you return with a qualifying one (you may take an immediate appeal to superior court under RSA 654:12, V). Affidavits can no longer be used to prove identity, age, or domicile at the polls — the challenged-voter and domicile affidavit options have been repealed (a qualified voter affidavit survives only to prove citizenship, under court order). If you don't have an approved photo ID, you can get one free, for voting purposes only, from any NH DMV office that issues IDs — ask your town/city clerk or the Secretary of State's office for the required voucher first.
voter_id.glance_value: Photo ID required (student ID not accepted; no affidavit option)
voter_id.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Election Day Voting
voter_id.internal_note: As of 2026-08-30, the codified RSA 659:13 text displayed at gc.nh.gov still includes subsection II(a)(5) permitting qualifying student ID — that page had not yet incorporated the 2026 amendment. Per user-confirmed research (2026-08-30): the New Hampshire General Court's enacted 2026 Chapter 243 (SB 223-FN), approved July 2, 2026, effective August 31, 2026, removes student ID from RSA 659:13's accepted voter-ID list; legislative history explicitly describes student ID as no longer accepted. The current NH SOS Election Day Voting page and the Sept-2026 SOS explanatory PDFs (#5-2026, #9-2026, #3-2026) already reflect this change and were used as the controlling sources for this section, per explicit source-hierarchy resolution from the user. Also per those same current SOS documents (not independently matched to a specific chapter number): the challenged-voter and domicile affidavit options for proving identity have been repealed; a qualified voter affidavit survives only to prove citizenship, under court order. Do not use the gc.nh.gov RSA 659:13 codification to contradict this section — re-check gc.nh.gov periodically to see whether it has been updated to match.

accessible_voting.label: Accessible Voting
accessible_voting.content: New Hampshire's Constitution (Part First, Article 11) requires every polling place to be accessible, and requires absentee voting to be available for anyone unable to vote in person due to disability. In practice, every polling place must have accessible parking (if there's a lot), a clear route from parking to an accessible entrance, and an accessible voting booth. Every polling place is also equipped with an accessible voting system — a tablet with a printer that lets a voter mark a ballot independently and privately using audio or an enhanced visual display. If you can't enter the polling place, an election official can bring you a ballot curbside using the absentee-voter procedure for an unforeseen accessibility issue. Any voter who needs help marking a ballot may ask the moderator for assistance from an election official or a person of their own choosing. If you have a print disability, you can apply for an Accessible Electronic Absentee Ballot to mark your ballot electronically at home (application updated effective September 30, 2025).
accessible_voting.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Voting with Disabilities

military_overseas.label: Military & Overseas Voting
military_overseas.content: If you're a qualified New Hampshire voter serving in the military or living overseas, you can register and request an absentee ballot using the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA) at fvap.gov, or by asking your local town/city clerk for one — the FPCA can register you and request your ballot at the same time. Your local clerk must receive your completed ballot by mail or commercial carrier by 5:00 p.m. on Election Day, and clerks are required by federal law to send ballots to UOCAVA voters at least 45 days before an election. An FPCA submitted in a given calendar year covers every state and municipal election that year, plus a presidential primary scheduled for the following year — submit a fresh one each year you plan to vote, and promptly after any address change. Track your ballot status anytime with the Voter Information Lookup.
military_overseas.source_name: NH Secretary of State — Uniformed and Overseas (UOCAVA) Voters

student_voting.label: College / Student Voting
student_voting.content: College students may lawfully register and vote where they attend school in New Hampshire, including using a dorm room as their domicile (RSA 654:1) — the same domicile rules apply to students as to any other resident: you can only have one voting domicile, and you can register wherever you've established your primary, ongoing presence for daily life, whether that's your campus address or your family home. Registering to vote in New Hampshire does not, by itself, require you to get an NH driver's license or register a vehicle here — those are separate motor vehicle law obligations that only apply if you actually drive or own a vehicle in the state, and they don't affect your right to register or vote (confirmed in joint guidance from the Secretary of State and Attorney General's Office). As with any voter, a student ID card cannot be used to satisfy either the registration or voting ID requirements — see Register to Vote and Voter ID Requirements above.
student_voting.source_name: RSA 654:1 (official NH statute text); joint SOS/Attorney General domicile guidance

sample_ballot.label: Official Sample Ballot
sample_ballot.content: The Secretary of State's Voter Information Lookup shows your official sample ballot for an upcoming election once it's finalized, using the same tool that looks up your polling place. If nothing appears for your address, contact your town or city clerk.

contact.label: Contact the State Election Authority
contact.content: New Hampshire Secretary of State, Elections Division — phone (603) 271-3242, fax (603) 271-6316, email elections@sos.nh.gov. Open Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–4:30 p.m. To report a suspected election-law violation, contact the New Hampshire Department of Justice's Election Law Unit (Attorney General's Civil Bureau) at (603) 271-3650, or the Election Law Hotline at 1-866-868-3703.

official_resources.label: Official State & Local Resources
official_resources.content: NH Secretary of State — Elections (sos.nh.gov/elections); the 2026–2027 Political Calendar for official state and town election dates; the Voters page (sos.nh.gov/elections/voters) for topic-by-topic guidance; and the Voter Information Lookup (app.sos.nh.gov), which provides local election and clerk contact information by town or city.
